Tajfel 1970: discrimination can be expected even if the individual is not involved in conflicts of interest and has no past history of hostility; it was enough for them to see themselves categorized into an ingroup and an outgroup.

Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan 2010 (Behav Brain Sci) abstract: behavioral scientists routinely publish broad claims about human psychology based on samples drawn entirely from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies.

Henrich et al. 2010 abstract: substantial variability in experimental results across populations; WEIRD subjects are particularly unusual, frequent outliers; among the least representative populations one could find for generalizing about humans.

Arnett 2008 (Am Psychol) abstract: research published in APA journals focuses too narrowly on Americans, who comprise less than 5% of the world's population; analysis of six premier APA journals shows samples are predominantly American.

Masuda and Nisbett 2001 (JPSP) abstract: Japanese and Americans watched animated vignettes of underwater scenes; the Japanese made more statements about contextual information and relationships than Americans did.

OpenStax 12.1: people from individualistic cultures, found in western countries such as the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, have the greatest tendency to commit the fundamental attribution error; collectivistic cultures focus on communal relationships.

Haslam and Reicher 2012 (PLoS Biol): participants tend to go along if the Experimenter justifies actions in terms of scientific benefits (the prod The experiment requires that you continue), but if he gives a direct order (You have no other choice, you must go on) participants typically refuse.

Haslam and Reicher 2012 abstract: individuals' willingness to follow authorities is conditional on identification with the authority in question and an associated belief that the authority is right, challenging the view that people conform passively.
OpenStax 11.7: Gordon Allport (Allport and Odbert, 1936) found 4,500 words in the English language that could describe people (the stable trait-term subset of a dictionary list).

OpenStax 11.7: each person has each factor, but they occur along a spectrum; most of us tend to lie somewhere midway along the continuum of each factor, rather than at polar ends.
OpenStax 11.9: self-report inventories use numbered scales from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree); increased likelihood of answering in ways that are more socially desirable.

Wikipedia (MBTI): constructed by Katharine Cook Briggs and her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers, inspired by Carl Jung's Psychological Types; after studying Jung's work; the Myers-Briggs Company facts page confirms Briggs and Myers as developers.
The Myers-Briggs Company MBTI facts: preferences in four pairs such as Extraversion or Introversion; sorting people into the 16 types.

Bess and Harvey 2002 (J Pers Assess), about 12,000 people: past reports of bimodality were artifacts; score distributions became strongly center-weighted; Wikipedia (MBTI): a cut-off line at the middle of each scale assigns opposite types.

McCrae and Costa 1989 abstract (Johns Hopkins portal): no support for the view that the MBTI measures truly dichotomous preferences; the four MBTI indices did measure aspects of four of the five major dimensions of normal personality.
OpenStax 7.5: reliability refers to a test's ability to produce consistent results.

Pittenger's own article (ERIC EJ475507) could not be opened in full.
California POST screening manual on the NEO PI-R: retest reliabilities for domain and facet scores ranged from 0.66 to 0.92 across samples and time frames ranging from weeks to years.
OpenStax 11.6: the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart conducted research with twins from 1979 to 1999; identical twins, whether raised together or apart, have very similar personalities.

Roberts, Walton and Viechtbauer 2006 (Psychol Bull) abstract: 92 samples; increases in social dominance, conscientiousness, and emotional stability, especially in young adulthood (age 20 to 40); agreeableness changed only in old age.

Roberts and DelVecchio 2000 (Psychol Bull) abstract: trait consistency increased from .31 in childhood to .54 during the college years, to .64 at age 30, and reached a plateau around .74 between ages 50 and 70.

Encyclopedia.com (Gale) Binet entries: in 1905, Binet and Theodore Simon created the first intelligence test to aid the French government in providing special education; the first Binet-Simon Scale was introduced in 1905.
OpenStax 7.5: the WISC-V's five indices are Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed, combined into a Full Scale IQ; the mean IQ score is 100.

Neisser et al. 1996 (Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns): tests are re-standardized from time to time; the mean score of the new standardization sample is typically set to 100 again; OpenStax 7.5: periodically normed and standardized as a means of recalibration.

Neisser et al. 1996: correlation between IQ scores and grades is about .50, accounting for only about 25% of the variance; school learning depends on persistence, interest in school, and willingness to study.
Neisser et al. 1996: the Flynn Effect is very well documented; the average gain is about three IQ points per decade (first described systematically by James Flynn).

Bratsberg and Rogeberg 2018 (PNAS) abstract: Norwegian conscription data; the Flynn effect, its turning point, and subsequent decline can all be fully recovered from within-family variation; title: Flynn effect and its reversal are both environmentally caused.
Neisser et al. 1996: the cause is presently unknown; interpretations include more complex daily life (children stay in school longer) and modern improvements in nutrition.
OpenStax 14.1: stress is a process whereby an individual perceives and responds to events that they appraise as overwhelming or threatening to their well-being (Lazarus and Folkman, 1984).

OpenStax 14.1: a primary appraisal involves judgment about the degree of potential harm or threat, appraised as a threat or a challenge; a secondary appraisal is judgment of the options available to cope and how effective such options will be.

OpenStax 14.1: if a person appraises an event as harmful and believes that the demands imposed by the event exceed the available resources to manage or adapt to it, the person will subjectively experience a state of stress.
OpenStax 14.1: eustress is a good kind of stress associated with positive feelings, optimal health, and performance; distress is excessive and debilitating, and performance begins to decline.

Berkeley lab paper reviewing the paradigm: Speisman, Lazarus, Mordkoff, and Davison (1964) both increased and decreased electrodermal responses to a stressful film by adding soundtracks that emphasized the traumatic nature, encouraged detachment, or emphasized positive aspects (PubMed 14136776 confirms the 1964 J Abnorm Psychol paper).
OpenStax 14.4: Coping refers to mental and behavioral efforts that we use to deal with problems relating to stress.
OpenStax 14.4: problem-focused coping addresses the problem (e.g., seek tutoring assistance); emotion-focused coping tries to change or reduce negative emotions (e.g., watch a comedy movie).

OpenStax 14.4: while many stressors elicit both kinds of coping, problem-focused coping is more likely with stressors we perceive as controllable, emotion-focused coping with stressors we believe we are powerless to change.

Park, Armeli and Tennen 2004 (PSPB) abstract: for 28 days, 190 undergraduates described their most stressful event; problem-focused coping had a stronger positive association with positive mood when dealing with high versus low control stressors.
Zakowski et al. 2001 abstract: Lazarus and Folkman's goodness-of-fit hypothesis (effects of coping moderated by appraised controllability) was partly confirmed.

Bonanno 2004 (Am Psychol): recovery connotes a trajectory in which normal functioning temporarily gives way to psychopathology, usually for at least several months, then returns; resilience, a stable trajectory of healthy functioning.

Bonanno 2004: resilient individuals may experience transient perturbations in normal functioning (e.g., several weeks of sporadic preoccupation or restless sleep) but generally exhibit a stable trajectory of healthy functioning.
Bonanno 2004: resilience to the unsettling effects of interpersonal loss is not rare but relatively common, does not appear to indicate pathology but rather healthy adjustment.

Bonanno et al. 2006 (Psychol Sci) abstract: probability sample of 2,752 New York area residents in the 6 months after September 11th; resilience in 65.1% of the sample; never fell below one third even among the most exposed groups.

Bonanno 2004: in a survey of self-identified bereavement experts, the majority (65%) endorsed beliefs that absent grief usually stems from denial or inhibition and is generally maladaptive in the long run (Middleton et al., 1993).
Bonanno 2004: most bereavement studies take place after the death already has occurred.

Bonanno 2004: prospective data gathered on average three years prior to the death of a spouse; 46% of the sample had low depression prior to the loss and through 18 months; not rated as emotionally cold or distant.
Bonanno 2004: no unequivocal evidence for delayed grief was found; even among resilient individuals, the majority reported experiencing at least some yearning and emotional pangs.

Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman 1978 abstract: 22 major lottery winners with 22 controls; lottery winners were not happier than controls and took significantly less pleasure from a series of mundane events.
Brickman et al. 1978 abstract: contrast with the peak experience of winning should lessen the impact of ordinary pleasures, while habituation should eventually reduce the value of new pleasures.
Lyubomirsky 2011 abstract: evidence for hedonic adaptation suggests that the joys of loves and triumphs and the sorrows of losses and humiliations fade with time.

Lucas 2007 (Current Directions) abstract: divorce, death of a spouse, unemployment, and disability are associated with lasting changes in SWB; considerable individual differences in the extent to which people adapt.

Diener and Seligman 2002 abstract: 222 undergraduates; compared the upper 10% of consistently very happy people with average and very unhappy people; stronger social relationships, more extraverted; did not experience more objectively defined good events.
problem: The fact is accurate, but card 088.c4 says the happiest 10 percent were compared "with everyone else"; the study compared them with an average group and a very unhappy group, not with all other students.
proposed: In 2002, Ed Diener and Martin Seligman compared the happiest 10 percent of 222 students with average and very unhappy students; the happiest had stronger social relationships and were more extraverted, but did not have more good events. (Card 088.c4 body: change "compared the happiest 10 percent of 222 students with everyone else" to "compared the happiest 10 percent of 222 students with average and very unhappy students".)

evidence: Diener and Seligman 2002 abstract: No variable was sufficient for happiness, but good social relations were necessary.

Diener and Seligman 2002 (DePaul-hosted copy): groups identified by an aggregate based on peer reports of affect, global self-reports collected on several occasions separated by months, and daily reports of affect over 51 days.

Wood, Quinn and Kashy 2002 (JPSP): between a third and a half of all behaviors listed were classified as habits, performed just about every day and usually in the same location; the estimate was greater in Study 2 (43%) than in Study 1 (35%); participants were signaled with a watch alarm each hour.
problem: Gives 43 percent as the result of the 2002 diary studies, but 43 percent is only the higher of the two studies; Study 1 found 35 percent, and the paper summarizes it as between a third and a half.
proposed: In 2002 diary studies led by Wendy Wood, between a third and a half of students' behaviors (35 percent in one study, 43 percent in the other) were done almost daily in the same place, often while thinking about something else. (Card 089.c1 body: change "About 43 percent of their behaviors were done almost daily in the same place" to "Between a third and a half of their behaviors were done almost daily in the same place". Card 090.c3, Habits point: change "About 43 percent of behaviors repeat daily in one place" to "A third to a half of behaviors repeat almost daily in one place".)

evidence: ScienceDaily (University of Bath, 2016): 800 adults in Peterborough (UK) received an intervention promoting sustainable behaviours or none, and had recently moved or not; a window of opportunity after relocation that lasted three months (Verplanken).

Gollwitzer and Sheeran 2006 abstract: holding a strong goal intention does not guarantee goal achievement; an implementation intention spells out the when, where, and how of goal striving in advance (If situation Y is encountered, then I will initiate goal-directed behavior X).

Gollwitzer and Sheeran 2006 abstract: findings from 94 independent tests showed implementation intentions had a positive effect of medium-to-large magnitude (d = .65) on goal attainment. The participant total (over 8,000) is widely reported but was not on an opened page; the scanned full text had no extractable text.
Gollwitzer and Sheeran 2006 abstract: implementation intentions were effective in promoting the initiation of goal striving, the shielding of ongoing goal pursuit from unwanted influences.

Roberts et al. 2007 (Perspectives on Psych Sci) abstract: the magnitude of the effects of personality traits on mortality, divorce, and occupational attainment was indistinguishable from the effects of SES and cognitive ability.
Roberts et al. 2007 abstract: only evidence from prospective longitudinal studies was considered; an attempt was made to limit the review to studies that controlled for important background factors.
WHO mental disorders fact sheet: In 2023, nearly 1 in every 7 people (1.2 billion) around the world were living with a mental disorder, with anxiety and depressive disorders the most common.
WHO fact sheet: A mental disorder is characterized by a clinically significant disturbance in an individual's cognition, emotional regulation, or behaviour.

American Psychiatric Association: Mental illnesses are health conditions involving changes in emotion, thinking or behavior; associated with distress and/or problems functioning in social, work or family activities.

OpenStax 15.1: just because something is atypical does not mean it is disordered; red hair is atypical but not disordered; disturbances do not reflect expected or culturally approved responses to events, such as grief after a death.

OpenStax 15.2: the DSM, published by the American Psychiatric Association; first edition published in 1952; DSM-5 (2013) and an updated DSM-5 Text Revision published in 2022; used by US mental health professionals.

OpenStax 15.2: the ICD, published by the World Health Organization; worldwide the ICD is more frequently used for clinical diagnosis, whereas the DSM is more valued for research (Mezzich, 2002).

Drescher 2015: DSM-I (1952) classified homosexuality as a sociopathic personality disturbance; Spitzer's criterion that disorders regularly caused subjective distress or generalized impairment, which homosexuality did not meet; the APA Board voted to remove it in December 1973.
OpenStax 15.4: anxiety motivates us to take actions, such as preparing for exams, that enable us to avert potential future problems; NIMH: feeling anxious is a normal part of life.
NIMH Anxiety Disorders: anxiety does not go away, is felt in many situations, and can get worse over time; symptoms can interfere with job performance, schoolwork, and relationships.

NIMH panic disorder page: if you think you're experiencing symptoms, talk to a health care provider, such as a primary care doctor, psychiatrist, psychologist, or clinical social worker; NIMH stress fact sheet: if symptoms of stress or anxiety won't go away, it may be time to talk to a professional; NIMH anxiety page: symptoms can interfere with daily life.
OpenStax 15.4: a panic attack is a period of extreme fear or discomfort that develops abruptly and reaches a peak within 10 minutes; symptoms include accelerated heart rate, sweating, trembling.

NIMH: people with panic disorder have frequent and unexpected panic attacks; many worry about the possibility of having another attack and may significantly change their lives to avoid having another attack.

Kessler et al. 2006 (Arch Gen Psychiatry, NCS-R) abstract: lifetime prevalence estimates are 22.7% for isolated panic without agoraphobia (PA only); OpenStax 15.4: around 23% of Americans experience isolated panic attacks without meeting criteria for panic disorder.
OpenStax 15.4: a specific phobia is excessive, distressing, and persistent fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation; out of proportion to the actual threat and often avoided.

NIMH Depression: Everyone feels sad or low sometimes, but these feelings usually pass. Depression (also called major depressive disorder) is different; severe symptoms that affect how a person feels, thinks, and handles daily activities, such as sleeping, eating, or working.
NIMH Depression: To be diagnosed with depression, a person must have symptoms most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks.
NIMH Depression: Research suggests that genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors play a role in the disorder.

Harvard Health: It's often said that depression results from a chemical imbalance, but that figure of speech doesn't capture how complex the disease is; many possible causes, including faulty mood regulation by the brain, genetic vulnerability, and stressful life events.

Moncrieff et al. (Mol Psychiatry, online July 2022) abstract: the main areas of serotonin research provide no consistent evidence of an association between serotonin and depression; King's College London response: methodological flaws, and the serotonin theory was not proposed as an imbalance in a single chemical.
Sullivan, Neale and Kendler 2000 (Am J Psychiatry) meta-analysis abstract: heritability of liability = 37%, 95% CI 31%-42%.

Cipriani et al. 2018 (Lancet) abstract: 522 trials comprising 116,477 participants; 21 antidepressant drugs; all antidepressants were more efficacious than placebo in adults with major depressive disorder.
King's College London: The decision to use antidepressants, with or without psychological therapy, is taken by the person with depression jointly with their treating physician.

NIMH ADHD: inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity; it is common for people to show these behaviors some of the time, but in ADHD they are frequent, occur across multiple situations and interfere with daily life; symptoms begin in childhood and usually continue into the teen years and adulthood.

NIMH: bipolar disorder causes clear shifts in a person's mood, energy, activity levels, and concentration; periods of extremely up, elated, irritable, or energized behavior (manic episodes) and very down periods (depressive episodes).

NIMH: common reactions after a traumatic event include feeling anxious and trouble concentrating and sleeping; most people will recover from these symptoms, and their reactions will lessen over time.

Royal College of Psychiatrists: CBT focuses on your current challenges rather than on your past experiences; CBT won't necessarily work for everyone, and alternatives exist. NHS: usually between 5 and 15 sessions; recommended for depression, anxiety including OCD, and PTSD.
Smith and Glass 1977 (American Psychologist): effect sizes computed from 375 studies; on the average, the typical therapy client is better off than 75% of untreated individuals.
Smith and Glass 1977 abstract: Few important differences in effectiveness could be established among many quite different types of psychotherapy.

American Psychiatric Association: harmful effects of stigma include reluctance to seek help or treatment and reduced likelihood of staying with treatment.

Center for Open Science: Registered Reports undergo peer review before results are known and are accepted in advance; eliminates questionable practices including low statistical power, selective reporting of results, and publication bias.

Center for Open Science: currently, over 300 journals use the Registered Reports publishing format; PubMed 23347556: Chambers 2013, Registered reports: a new publishing initiative at Cortex (Cortex 49(3), 2013).

The Psychologist (BPS): Cuddy's talk remains the second-most watched TED Talk of all time.
